name: Facial growth guidance appliances (Biobloc / Twin Block)

lead: Facial growth guidance appliances are devices used while a child is still growing to steer jaw development toward a better-balanced face and profile. The Biobloc is John Mew's system from the orthotropics tradition; the Twin Block is a functional appliance from mainstream orthodontics.

In looksmaxxing circles they are discussed as a way to shape the face while growth is still possible. Mew's approach uses a palate-expanding appliance followed by a postural appliance, on the idea that oral posture shapes facial growth, and the Twin Block encourages forward jaw posture during growth. Mainstream bodies say evidence for orthotropic efficacy is inadequate; sources on the specific effects are thin.

paras: An orthodontist fits the appliance during childhood or early teens, and it is worn for set hours daily over months, sometimes followed by braces.

No source reviewed documents specific risks for these appliances. Mike Mew, a promoter of the orthotropic approach, faced a misconduct hearing over harm to child patients. Appliances generally need professional supervision.

angle.text: Parents and orthotropics followers use growth guidance appliances in children to steer jaw development toward a better-balanced face. Twin Block is a mainstream functional appliance, while Biobloc belongs to the orthotropics camp, and research on its facial effects is limited.

lead: Facial growth guidance appliances are orthodontic devices used in growing patients with the aim of directing jaw and facial development. They are used to widen the palate, bring the lower jaw forward and encourage a more forward, balanced facial profile and a better bite while the bones are still growing.[1][1] The term is associated with orthotropics, the approach founded by John Mew, whose treatment system, the Biobloc, uses a palate-expanding appliance followed by a postural appliance.[1]

The Twin Block, a removable functional appliance from conventional orthodontics, consists of upper and lower acrylic bite blocks with inclined planes that lock together and guide the lower jaw forward and down. It is used in children and adolescents with Class II malocclusion, in which the lower jaw sits behind the upper.[2] Looksmaxxing forums group Biobloc, Twin Block, Herbst and Bionator appliances together when discussing ways to change the lower third of the face.[3]

Mew helped found the International Association of Facial Growth Guidance in 1987.[1] Mainstream orthodontic bodies say evidence for orthotropic efficacy is inadequate, while published studies from Biobloc practitioners report favorable soft-tissue, growth-direction and airway measurements.[1][1][4][5][6]
infobox: Removable functional appliance for Class II malocclusion[2]

paras: Wikipedia describes the Biobloc as John Mew's treatment system, using a palate-expanding appliance followed by a postural appliance as part of orthotropics.[1] The wider theory holds that tongue and oral posture shape the face.[1] Mew developed the approach after his 1958 Tropic Premise, which called malocclusion a postural deformity, and argued that environment rather than genetics mainly determines crooked teeth, a view that mainstream orthodontics does not share.[1]

The General Dental Council reprimanded Mew in 2010 over advertisements with misleading assertions, and revoked his licence to practise in 2017 over false advertising claims and breaching patient confidentiality. The British Orthodontic Society expelled his son Michael Mew around 2019.[1] A 2019 review in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery found some plausible conclusions in the theory but inadequate evidence for the treatment's efficacy.[1]

sections.h: Twin Block and other functional appliances
paras: A 2014 systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 controlled studies of short-term Twin Block treatment in mild-to-moderate Class II division 1 malocclusion, treated for 8 to 16 months, reported tipping of the lower incisors forward and upper incisors back, and increases in mandibular length and forward mandibular position. Maxillary growth was not clinically restrained, and lower face height also increased. The authors judged most individual changes to be of limited clinical significance but the combined changes to be clinically important, and noted that only short-term outcomes were assessed.[2]

A commentary on the review notes that a Cochrane review of 17 randomized trials of functional appliances found similar skeletal changes that were not clinically significant, and the Twin Block review's own authors noted that the largest low-bias study found no significant skeletal changes.[2]

Looksmax.org members have posted about widening the palate with Biobloc-type appliances, including a thread in which a poster gives a pre-treatment palate width of about 50 mm and plans a 4 to 6 mm expansion, and a thread asking whether Herbst, Twin Block and Bionator appliances work for the lower third.[3][7] Orthodontic sources describe these appliances as designed for use while growth is ongoing in children and adolescents.[2]

A 2009 controlled study of 41 cases (30 treated, 11 untreated controls) used landmarks on lateral photographs and found soft-tissue changes in Biobloc-treated patients showed a consistent growth direction of about 45 degrees, versus a more vertical and less consistent direction in untreated patients; the authors concluded this is consistent with a more balanced profile.[4] A 2001 pilot study of 12 patients with overjets above 10 mm compared fixed retraction with removable orthotropic appliances, reporting a mean growth direction at gnathion of 67 degrees for fixed appliances versus 46 degrees for Biobloc.[5] A 2007 study of 53 children (mean age 12.9) reported relative increases in nasopharyngeal (31 percent), oropharyngeal (23 percent) and hypopharyngeal (9 percent) airway area after Biobloc therapy,[6] and a 2016 study of 64 children aged 7 to 12 with Class I malocclusion treated with Biobloc appliances examined upper airway patency.[8] A small 2007 study of 12 pairs of identical twins compared orthotropic treatment with fixed appliances using lay judges to rate facial changes. Wikipedia reports that evidence for orthotropic efficacy is considered inadequate.[1]
